# Tetrahedral serial multiview microscopy and image fusion for improved resolution and extent in stained zebrafish embryos

**Authors:** Johanna B. Kroll; Anna Cha; Alon Oyler-Yaniv; Talley Lambert; Ian A. Swinburne; Andrew Murphy; Sean G. Megason

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Systems Biology, Harvard Medical School, 200 Longwood Ave., Boston, MA 02115 | 2University of Muenster, Muenster, Germany | 3Department of Molecular Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley, CA

## Abstract

Spatial mapping on the single cell level over the whole organism can uncover roles of molecular players involved in vertebrate development. Custom microscopes have been developed that use multiple objectives to view a sample from multiple views at the same time. Such multiview imaging approaches can improve resolution and uniformity of image quality as well as allow whole embryos to be imaged.1 However, multiview imaging is highly restricted to specialized equipment requiring multiple objectives or sample rotation with automated hardware.

Our approach uses a standard single objective confocal microscope to perform serial multiview imaging (SMIM). Multiple views are imaged sequentially by mounting the fixed sample in an agarose tetrahedron that is manually rotated in between imaging each face. Computational image fusion allows for a joint 3D image to be created from multiple tiled z-stacks acquired from different angles. The resulting fused image has improved resolution and imaging extent.

With this technique, multiview imaging can be performed on a variety of common single objective microscopes to allow for whole embryo, high-resolution imaging.

## Introduction

Understanding spatial patterns of localization of mRNAs, proteins, and other molecules often lays the groundwork for many questions in biology. Fluorescence microscopy is a main tool to image these patterns in diverse tissues. However, detection of fluorescently labeled molecules over large and thick samples, such as zebrafish embryos and other model systems often used in developmental biology, is limited by multiple factors. These include the microscope’s field of view, resolution in Z, light scattering of the specimen, and bleaching through repeated fluorophore excitation. In live imaging, the imaging speed and phototoxicity pose additional restrictions.2,3 While advances in various microscope systems address these limitations, there is still a lack of a versatile tool to capture spatial patterns in toto over a large and deep tissue with good resolution.

Multiview imaging approaches have emerged to improve coverage of thick samples at high resolution. By imaging the sample from multiple directions, views where the tissue of interest is most superficial can be selected. This enhances resolution and signal-to-noise by reducing light scattering artefacts. Additionally, angled views can improve the Z resolution as the better lateral resolution compensates for the poorer axial resolution.1,4 In Multiple Imaging Axis Microscopy (MIAM), one of the first systems for multiview imaging, four identical objectives are arranged in a tetrahedral geometry to overcome limitations in Z resolutions and to improve image quality by combining Point Spread Functions (PSFs) of multiple views.5 Other multiview imaging approaches, such as DiSPIM, TriSPIM, and multiSPIM.4,6,7 use two or more objectives, switching between excitation and detection, to generate views from multiple angles. This enables fast live imaging as views can be captured simultaneously. Alternatively, or additionally, samples can be mounted in a cylinder to allow automated 360° rotation in a sample holder.4 Mounting for live imaging requires refined strategies to ensure normal development while keeping the sample fixed enough for image reconstruction.8 More recently, multiview imaging with one objective, DaXi, was introduced. DaXi uses oblique illumination through one objective which can be switched for multiple illumination angles and simplifies sample mounting by using a single objective setup (Yang et al., 2022). Whole zebrafish embryos have been imaged with a multiview lightsheet setup with four lenses and the DaXi setup at single cell resolution for an extended period of time.9,10 A recently published atlas made multiple extensive datasets of the early development of zebrafish embryos acquired with DaXi and OpenSiMView system openly available.11 Multiview imaging has been used on other model organisms including C. elegans and Drosophila.9,12 While most of the advances for multiview imaging involve light-sheet microscopy, a confocal-based multiview system was developed as well (Wu et al., 2021). They utilized compact line scanners together with multiview imaging to reduce phototoxicity, while improving lateral and axial resolution over a millimeter spatial scale.

These methods can achieve high resolution volumetric imaging of large and thick samples, but a major barrier to these techniques is their high complexity and need for customized assembly of these microscopes for a particular sample type. Here we present a mounting solution for sequential multiview imaging that can be adapted to routinely available single-objective microscopes such as confocal. Samples are embedded in an agarose tetrahedron and rotated manually between imaging acquisitions. The different sides are imaged separately from a single objective to capture Z-stacks (or tiled Z-stacks) from each of the four faces and then computationally reconstructed to achieve whole specimen, 3D, high resolution images. We demonstrate this tetrahedral image fusion approach using laser scanning and spinning disk confocal microscopy to in toto image zebrafish embryos. Unlike other multiview imaging systems, this imaging strategy can be adapted for upright and inverted imaging setups independent of the microscope system, allowing for a versatile, widely-useable application. Furthermore, it can be adapted for use with different mounting media such as tissue clearing and refractive index matching.

## Results

### Tetrahedral mounting and imaging allows for whole embryo reconstruction at cellular level

We used 3d printing to make an acrylic plastic template containing an array of tetrahedra of various sizes affixed to a plane. This template was then used to cast a PDMS mold consisting of an array of tetrahedral wells (Fig. 1A). To mount samples, they are placed in molten agarose, and then transferred one sample per well in agarose into the mold. The tetrahedral mold is designed for samples to be contained completely inside the tetrahedron but still close to all four faces (Fig. 1B). Once the agarose has set, the sample can be removed from the mold, mounted, and the tetrahedron imaged from all faces (Fig. 1C,D). We term this approach Serial Multiview Imaging (SMIM). Here, we focus on tetrahedral SMIM because it minimizes the number of required views and fits early zebrafish embryos, but other shapes may be more appropriate for different samples. The shape of the mount should resemble the shape of the sample to ensure minimal negative space that has to be covered by imaging.

For testing, we injected transgenic tg(actb2:memb-mNeonGreen) zebrafish embryos with mRNA encoding Histone2B-mCherry into 1 cell at the 2-cell to 8-cell stage to generate embryos expressing the red fluorescent histone marker mosaically and the green fluorescent membrane marker ubiquitously. After fixation at 18hpf, the embryos were embedded in an agarose tetrahedron together with multi-colored 0.2 μm fluorescent beads. We imaged from the four sides of the tetrahedron, rotating it between imaging each side (Fig. 1E) on an upright confocal point scanning microscope. Since imaging a tetrahedron on an upright microscope requires the point to be down, we also used 3d printing to make a PDMS mount to hold the agarose tetrahedra point-side-down while imaging and to allow for ordered flipping between faces (Fig. 1C). When imaging with 20X magnification, each side was imaged with 2×2 tiled Z-stacks as it allows for a wider field of view which increases the overlap of sides for reconstruction. Bleaching can occur between tiles and sides depending on imaging conditions which is visible as grid lines in the reconstructed embryo. We fused the four views using the Fiji plug-in BigStitcher (Fig.1 F,G)13 with the fluorescent beads as registration points (Fig. 2A,B) (Suppl. Video 1–3). We assessed the level of alignment visually by comparing how well the membrane signal and nuclei signal collected from different views overlap (Fig. 2C,D). While there is not perfect alignment in subcellular structures like the membrane, the registration achieves cellular level alignment visible in the nuclei channel (Fig. 2D). The multiview imaging approach improves spatial extent to full coverage of an 18 hpf embryo, but signal attenuation in depth can still be an issue (Fig. 2C).

To test the limits of registration, we also reconstructed the four views from a sample that we know got distorted during sample handling and subsequent imaging. We compared the registration of this distorted sample to a normal sample. With sufficient overlap of imaging area containing fluorescent beads, registration of multiple angles works robustly, even when the tetrahedron is mildly damaged or deformed due to suboptimal handling (suppl. Fig. 1).

### Spatial error plotting allows visual assessment of image fusion quality

We wanted to assess the spatial variation in the accuracy of image fusion by plotting the distance between points of interest mapped from different views. BigStitcher has a built-in error metric, which calculates the average pixel error after registration. It is not suitable in this case because multicolored beads in different channels within same tiles are registered to each other. Therefore, the calculated error from BigStitcher might not correspond to the real error of the multiview reconstruction. Instead, we developed our own error metric using a python script that calculates the registration error between selected sides and tiles within one channel. The script uses the coordinates of corresponding beads to calculate the distance between them after registration to allow for spatial error plotting (Fig. 1H). In normal datasets the average pixel error is ~ 4 px (Fig. 3A). With a voxel width of 0.59 μm after registration this registration error corresponds to 2.4 μm. This confirms that the registration accuracy is on a cellular level as also seen in the nuclei channel.

We also plotted the error distribution of normal and distorted datasets (Fig. 3B). Distorted datasets have some beads with small matching errors like the normal datasets, but contain more beads with high errors resulting in a higher average error and flattened error distribution (Fig. 3B). We chose a dataset from each of the two groups to visualize the error distribution in 3d space (Suppl. Video 4, 5). Each dot represents a corresponding interest point pair with color coded error. In normal samples, the error is lower in all regions of the sample with some outliers to the edge of the tetrahedron (Fig. 3C). This is likely due to displacement of beads during the manual rotation of the tetrahedron. Since the beads are in the surrounding agarose there is no representation of error distribution within the sample. In distorted datasets, regions of good and bad registration accuracy can be seen throughout the sample (Fig. 3D).

### Fluorescent in situ hybridization patterns can be mapped onto the embryo in 3d using tetrahedral SMIM

We next attempted to map gene expression patterns in the whole embryo using tetrahedral SMIM. We performed HCR fluorescent in-situ hybridization for her15.1 and col1a1a in 18hpf tg(actb2:mNeonGreen;shh:GFP) embryos14 (Fig. 4). We chose these two probes for their known expression closer to the surface of the embryo to eliminate potential loss of signal in depth. The sample was imaged on an upright confocal laser scanning microscope with 20X water immersion objective with a working distance of 1.8 mm resulting in about 400 μm stacks imaged in 2×2 tiles per view. The expression patterns of col1a1a and her15.1 were visualized in 3d with napari (Fig. 4) (Suppl. Video 6–8).

### CUBIC clearing can be adapted to SMIM

One approach to address signal attenuation with depth is to reduce light scattering in the sample by tissue clearing. The CUBIC clearing method is simple consisting of soaking in two solutions: CUBIC-L for “delipidation” and CUBIC-R for refractive index matching.15,16 Soaking 18hpf embryos with CUBIC-L led to an increase in transparency in the yolk but no measurable change in the tissue (Fig. 5A,B). CUBIC-L soaking for longer than 1 h did not lead to a further increase in transparency (Fig. 5B) while treatment that lasts longer than 24 hours lead to yolks rupturing (data not shown) due to swelling of the yolk. To assess whether swelling affects the tissue morphology, we measured the size of the yolk and tailbud and found that the swelling is restricted to the yolk (Fig. 5C–E). We measured the otic vesicle in a 24hpf embryo to examine the effect of yolk swelling on this lumenized structure that is easily deformed. The otic vesicle is distorted in the medial-lateral axis, but the overall volume does not increase (Fig. 5F–I). Distortion in the medial-lateral axis could be explained by the strong swelling of the yolk compared to the tissue.

The most drastic change in transparency is visible when comparing the embryo before and after refractive index matching with CUBIC-R (Fig. 5A). CUBIC-R led to a rapid and strong clearing of the embryo either alone or in combination with CUBIC-L. We conclude that CUBIC-R is a simple and effective means for clearing zebrafish embryos. CUBIC-L does improve transparency of the yolk, but at the cost of swelling and potential tissue deformation. We also note, that based on the yolk swelling and the lack of reduction in Nile Red staining of the yolk (data not shown), CUBIC-L does not seem to extract lipids from the yolk as implied by the term “delipidation” but rather homogenizes their refractive index in the yolk.

### Refractive index matching improves signal attenuation with depth

We then compared the effect of refractive index matching and delipidation on signal attenuation. We compared control and delipidated embryos imaged in PBST and embryos that were subsequently treated with CUBIC-R for refractive index-matching and imaged in the same solution (Fig. 6A). The signal attenuation with depth was quantified in a selected rectangular region of interest by calculating mean intensities per Z slice in tg(actb2:mNeonGreen;shh:GFP) 18 hpf embryos (Fig. 6B). For each condition, we fit an exponential decay curve normalized to their respective maximum. Fitted decay constants show that all three conditions – control, 1h CUBIC-L and 3h CUBIC-L – show the same range of values, whereas all conditions without CUBIC-R show a higher rate of scattering compared to CUBIC-R conditions (Fig. 6C). Importantly, for most embryos imaged in CUBIC-R, no decay with depth could be fit because the signal drop off was minimal. Image quality decays only minimally with depth when using CUBIC-R, while in normal conditions the image quality drastically decreased within the first 150 μm (Fig. 6A).

The effect of clearing seen in brightfield images, where the increase in transparency was greatest in embryos immersed in CUBIC-R, (Fig. 5A) holds for fluorescence microscopy. Delipidated embryos showed increase in transparency mostly in the yolk (Fig. 5B), which may explain the lack of improvement in signal attenuation with delipidation in the tissue. Thus, while CUBIC-L does improve transparency of the yolk, for many applications CUBIC-R alone can be used since it substantially improves transparency without CUBIC-L which can distort tissue due to yolk swelling.

### Combining clearing with multiview imaging improves gene expression pattern mapping

We performed tetrahedral imaging on refractive index matched embryos to determine whether the improvement in signal attenuation could benefit mapping of gene expression patterns deeper in the tissue. Combing refractive index matching with the tetrahedral imaging requires an objective which is matched to the CUBIC-R index of refraction while still having a work distance long enough to focus deep into the tetrahedron. For that, we used an inverted confocal spinning disc with a 20X glycerol objective which has a working distance of 330 μm allowing an average of 200–230 μm stack size to be acquired. For imaging on an inverted microscope, the agarose tetrahedra can simply be placed on a coverslip bottom dish (Fig. 1C). This result shows that tetrahedral imaging can be adapted to a variety of different microscope setups.

We compared HCR-FISH imaging for flt4 and myod1 with and without CUBIC-R refractive index matching. Due to the different available objectives required for the different refractive indexes, we used a spinning disc confocal with CUBIC-R and laser scanning confocal without CUBIC-R (Fig. 7A–D). Expression of flt4 appears clearer in the refractive index matched sample (Fig. 7A,C). Comparing cross sections of the registered images, the flt4 gene expression pattern in the deeper tissues in the head and tail is fully captured in the cleared sample, whereas in the non-cleared sample the signal attenuates with depth (Fig. 7B,D,E). The signal to noise ratio for flt4 was better in the image acquired in CUBIC-R. We conclude that refractive index matching improves signal attenuation in depth (Fig.6, Fig. 7F), but we note that the upright confocal and inverted spinning disc have different available objectives and detectors. Notably, the higher index-of-refraction objective used on the spinning disc set up has a reduced working distance, allowing acquisition of about half the stack size of what could be acquired on the laser-scanning confocal microscope (Fig. 7B,D). Additionally, the spinning disc microscope had a shorter acquisition time for three channels per slice of 0.5 s whereas the point scanner takes 8 s per slice. Also, the spinning disc data have a smaller pixel size, which results in a voxel width of 0.32 μm. However, the registration accuracy is comparable with the laser-scanning microscope. The dataset shown in Fig. 7C has an average pixel error of 5.02 px or 1.6 μm. The reduced working distance of the spinning disc leads to a region in the middle of the embryo that cannot be covered. In the cross section of the registered image, the shorter working distance is clearly visible as an uncaptured tetrahedron shaped cutout in the middle (Fig. 7E). The missing information is mostly in the yolk, which does not affect registration nor most of the expression pattern, but there are small parts of the tissue missing in the head. Because of the shape of zebrafish embryo and how it sits in the tetrahedron, one tip of the uncaptured region may contain a part of a tissue when working with shorter working distance objectives.

## Discussion

We present Serial Multiview Imaging (SMIM), a pipeline for mounting, imaging, and image fusion to achieve in toto reconstruction of zebrafish embryos at cellular resolution by imaging samples embedded in agarose tetrahedra from all four sides. Using open-source software, Big Stitcher, and different commonly available microscopes, we can register multiple views to reconstruct embryo-wide gene expression patterns.

There are some critical steps to achieve optimal reconstruction results. Sample handling steps – casting, mounting, and turning the tetrahedron – require more care than the downstream processing steps. During these steps, the user should take care to not damage or put pressure on the tetrahedron which may introduce distortion. The imaging system needs a motorized stage and focus to preserve geometrical properties during tiling in XY as well as in the Z direction to accurately represent sides during reconstruction. Failure in the downstream processing steps can result if imaging settings do not allow sufficient coverage in XY and Z.

We showed that the reconstruction of the four views is possible with low pixel error and that even with a distorted sample, the reconstruction can work to some degree, albeit with higher pixel error. The registration error makes this method not suitable for multiview deconvolution in downstream processing. However, since the error is low enough to accurately reconstruct a zebrafish on cellular level, it can still be used to visualize whole embryo expression patterns. Although, not implemented here, we expect that subsequent deformable registration would yield further improvements.

Once we determined that multi-view tetrahedral imaging works, we attempted to further optimize the sample for imaging. We show that using refractive index matching with CUBIC-R with or without CUBIC-L reduces signal attenuation with depth to accurately image gene expression deeper in the tissue. Immersion media can introduce softening or deformation to the tetrahedron potentially resulting in distortion and should therefore only be used when introducing a benefit in signal attenuation in depth.

Additionally, we adapted the method for multiple imaging setups. We have compared results from two different microscopes: upright point scanning confocal and inverted spinning disc confocal. There are advantages and disadvantages to each set up. The spinning disc is much faster during acquisition than the confocal laser scanning microscope, and with the combination of CUBIC-R and a high index-of-refraction objective, it has a better signal to noise ratio. The confocal laser scanning microscope can handle out of focus light better, which helps with widespread labels that can cause haze in other setups. Additionally, setting up the sample for imaging on an upright and on an inverted microscope differs. For the upright scope, the set up requires an imaging mold that will hold the tetrahedron in place. For the inverted microscope, a coverglass-bottomed dish can be used in which the tetrahedron is submerged in water or a refractive index matching solution. The upright mounting method provides a more robust and stable mount, which makes the acquisition and tiling easier than mounting for an inverted scope. Both upright and inverted microscopes can be used to gather optimal images for reconstruction.

Compared to other multiview methods, the mounting solution presented here has limitations in accuracy. Using lightsheet microscopes, it is possible to achieve subpixel registration accuracy with multiview imaging for some areas of the sample.17 However current multiview lightsheet approaches do not space the views equally in 3d (on all faces of a Platonic solid) resulting in some areas of the sample being covered better than others. Downstream processing like multiview deconvolution relies on this subpixel accuracy. Therefore, the imaging approach presented here is not suitable for multiview deconvolution at present. Acquisition of a multiview stack in a four-lens SPIM of a 400 slice stack with multiview imaging takes 30 s10, whereas acquisition of a 400 slice stack on the spinning disc takes 27 min and on the confocal laser scanning microscope up to 4 h. Together with embedding in high-strength agarose, this makes the present mounting solution not suitable for live imaging. Due to repeated laser exposure, bleaching must be assessed individually for each sample and laser settings as well as sample conditions need to be optimized.

Compared to regular confocal imaging, multiview imaging enables sample coverage which would not be possible with shorter working distance objectives for matching higher refractive indices and with high numerical apertures. The working distance of 330 μm could not cover the whole zebrafish embryo, but with the tetrahedral SMIM and CUBIC-R clearing, in toto imaging can be achieved without signal attenuation in depth for visualizing the full embryo.

In conclusion, we provide a versatile tool to make multiview in toto imaging of fixed samples more accessible by using a cheap and easy mounting approach, commonly available microscope setups, and open-source software. Using fixed samples the method could contribute to better mapping of FISH as it allows in toto visualization in 3d. The method can be adapted to different samples like younger zebrafish embryos or other organisms whose geometry is suited for tetrahedron mounting and imaging. Alternatively, different shapes and sizes of agarose can be used for embryos more suited to other shapes.

## Experimental Procedures

### Zebrafish lines

Wildtype: AB fish, tg(actb2:mNeonGreen) and tg(shh:GFP)18.

Zebrafish husbandry and experimental usage were approved by the Harvard Medical School Animal Care and Use Committee (Protocol number: 04487) and performed in accordance with the guidelines. Adult zebrafish were maintained on a 14 h light / 10 h dark cycle at ~28 °C. The following fish genotypes were used: tg(actb2:mNeonGreen) for fluorescence labeling of the membrane. Those fish were generated by DNA injection and selection for brightness which led to a multiple copy line. Tg(shh:GFP) fish were used to fluorescently label Shh expressing cells (Shkumatava et al., 2004). “Wildtype” (WT) refers to AB zebrafish from the Zebrafish International Resource Center (ZIRC).

### Sample preparation

Embryos were manually dechorionated as the use of Pronase enzyme was not suitable for CUBIC-L treatment and subsequent swelling. 18 hpf zebrafish embryos were fixed in 4% PFA in PBS for 24h at 4°C. For HCR, embryos were fixed 24h in 4% PFA at 4°C. After stopping the fixation with 3×5 min washes with PBST at RT, the embryos were dehydrated in 100% methanol 4×10 min and 1×50 min and permeabilized at −20 °C for 24 h. Embryos can be stored in methanol at −20 °C. For staining, HCR protocol (version 3.0) was used.14 A detailed version of the performed steps and concentrations can be found here.19 When expression patterns were known, Alexa-647 was used for higher gene expression as it is more sensitive to bleaching. All buffers were used with 0.1% Tween to ensure that embryos don’t stick to the wall.

### CUBIC protocol with 18 hpf old zebrafish embryos

Embryos at 18 hpf were fixed using the protocol stated in sample preparation. Older embryos at 24 hpf were fixed for 2h at RT in 4% PFA, permeabilized with acetone for 7 min at −20 °C and then delipidated for 1 h with CUBIC-L to ensure that other more sensitive tissue structures are not affected.20

Embryos were gradually rehydrated to PBST. 5 min 75%, 50% and 25% MeOH (in PBST) and 5×5min 100% PBST. For delipidation, embryos were incubated 15 min in 50% CUBIC-L at 37°C and in 100% CUBIC-L for 1–3 h. CUBIC-L was removed by washing in PBST 3x for 15 min. CUBIC-L treatment was always performed before HCR protocol, since CUBIC-L removes hairpin fluorescence. After sample staining right before imaging, embryos were incubated in 50% CUBIC-R at RT for 15 min and in 100% CUBIC-R for 1–3h. Brightfield images were acquired on an Olympus MVX10 stereoscope equipped with a MV PLAPO 2X lens together with AxioCam MRc camera and the AxioVision software (release 4.8.2 SP3 (08–2013)). Brightness levels were adjusted for each experiment and kept consistent between images.

For mapping signal attenuation with depth, embryos were mounted dorsally, and the anterior neural tube was imaged. A region of interest was determined and mean intensities were plotted over Z.

All data are plotted using GraphPad Prism 8.0.1. Curves are fitted using Nonlinear regression, one phase decay. Statistical tests are performed as indicated using GraphPad Prism 8.0.1.

### Template design and PDMS mount casting

Templates were designed in Blender (blender.org) and 3d printed by Shapeways (shapeways.com) out of “fine detail plastic” material (acrylic) using Material Jetting as the 3d printing method. The blender and STL files for the templates are open-source and can be found https://github.com/smegason/SMIM. The templates can be ordered at Shapeways (https://www.shapeways.com/shops/megason-lab). While designing the templates for casting and imaging mounts, both mounts were coordinated with each other. The size of the tetrahedron is dependent on the size of the sample and on the working distance of the objective used in the imaging setup. The working distance needs to be large enough to generate overlap between the different sides of the tetrahedron. Here, the height of the tetrahedron of the casting mount is 1.4 mm. The imaging mount for upright setups was adapted to the size of the casting mount. The depth of the tetrahedral wells in the imaging mount was slightly smaller than the casting mount such that tetrahedra could be removed and re-oriented. Four tetrahedral wells were arranged in a row for tracking the imaged sides and to simplify the moving of the tetrahedron from one well into the next. The walls around the well were designed to be high enough that when the agarose tetrahedron sits in the well, it is still smaller than the walls. This ensured that a coverslip doesn’t put pressure on the tetrahedron when it is added on top of the walls.

The templates were used to cast the PDMS mounts using the SYLGARD™ 184 Silicon Elastomer Kit from the Dow Chemical Company. PDMS mounts were plasma cleaned and stored in 10% Polyethylene glycol (PEG) in milliQ H2O (Fig. 1A)

### Tetrahedron Casting

Bead stock solution was prepared by diluting 0.2 μm TetraSpeck™ beads 1:10 in milliQ H2O after sonicating. The final dilution within the tetrahedron should be 1:1000. When other beads are used the concentration should be adjusted to 10–50 visible beads per Z slice. Beads can be stored at 4°C but need to be sonicated before every use. 1% high strength agarose in milliQ water was prepared and stored at 55 °C. The stock can be used for 4–5 days before quality declines. Right before mounting the PDMS mount for casting the tetrahedron was washed with water and warmed up in an open petri dish to 55 °C. Washing is a critical step as it makes the mount more repellent and allows for easy removal of the agarose tetrahedron. An embryo was transferred to an Eppendorf tube, excess liquid removed and 2 μL of 1:10 TetraSpeck™ bead dilution added to the side of the tube. After adding 198 μL of 1% agarose to the embryo, mixing by pipetting up and down once, the embryo was transferred in an agarose drop on top of the warmed-up PDMS mount next to a tetrahedral mount. After removing any air bubbles within the tip of a tetrahedral well using forceps, the embryo was gently pushed into the tetrahedral well, and excess agarose was scraped of using a razor blade. The mounting process was performed as fast as possible (2 min), before the agarose sets. The orientation of the embryo was not adjusted within the tetrahedron. The excess agarose drop which was scraped off the top was tested for solidification and after up to 4 min the agarose tetrahedron was removed by picking up and bending the PDMS mount. This loosens the agarose from the PDMS mount. A hair tool or a micro-loader pipette tip was used to gently move the agarose tetrahedron out of the PDMS mount and transferred to the imaging setup. After the initial solidification step in air, the agarose tetrahedron was kept in PBST or CUBIC-R to avoid drying out (Fig. 1B).

### Tetrahedron Mounting and Flipping for upright setups with water immersion

The PDMS imaging mount was washed with tap water to remove as much of the PEG as possible. Around 60–100 μL of 1x PBST was added to the mount and air bubbles were removed from the tetrahedral well. The prepared agarose tetrahedron was transferred to the mount and placed in the first well. A coverslip was carefully added from the side by tilting it on top of the mount. Sliding of the coverglass was avoided as it causes friction and distortion in the tetrahedron. Air bubbles must be avoided. The coverglass helps keep the tetrahedron in place, while not adding pressure as it is supported by the walls of the mount. The coverglass is required for the objective we used but other objectives may not. Water for immersion was added on top of the coverglass. Between sides, the tetrahedron was flipped for multiview imaging. For that, the coverslip was removed, the tetrahedron carefully flipped to the next side and the coverslip was added again. The flipping took about 3–5 minutes. Notes were kept on the sides already imaged to avoid imaging one side twice (Fig. 1C–E).

### Tetrahedron Mounting and Flipping for inverted setups with refractive index matching

A glass bottom dish was prepared by adding 20–40 μL of 100% CUBIC-R in the middle of the dish. The agarose tetrahedron was added and submerged for 10–15 min before imaging. A fully refractive-index-matched agarose tetrahedron sinks to the bottom. Right before imaging most of the CUBIC-R was removed so that only the tip of the tetrahedron was showing. This keeps the tetrahedron submerged and in place while imaging. The “top” of the dish was marked and one side adjusted to it. Between sides, more CUBIC-R was added to freely flip the tetrahedron to the next side. The tetrahedron was flipped two times to the left and one time to the right to keep track of the sides and ensure that all four sides were imaged. ### Imaging recommendations for SMIM

When choosing an objective, it should be considered that accurate Z stack acquiring is necessary, meaning that lower magnification (NA) objectives with poor Z-section thickness should not be used.

A water or glycerol objective with a higher NA would be preferrable. An objective with a larger working distance helps to generate more overlap between views which can help to get the full spatial extent of larger embryos. For acquisition, decide on bit depth which is sufficient for the respective imaging system. Camera based systems can resolve 16-bit whereas for most point scanner systems 8-bit is enough and will reduce the file size. Try to keep the imaging time to a minimum by adjusting the imaging settings accordingly. For example, for point scanning images use 1024×1024 pixel, line averaging 4 and adjust the laser intensities to a lower level. Antifading can be used, but it needs to match the used refractive index. Some antifading reagents soften the agarose which can introduce distortion. During acquisition in upright setup, the PDMS mount can autofluoresce which can later interfere with the registration of the multiple views. If autofluorescence around the tetrahedron is visible, stop the Z stack before imaging the PDMS. The Z stack and tiling needs to generate enough overlap between sides for registration. For example, a stack size of 400 μm and 2×2 tiling worked well.

### Post processing with BigStitcher and visualization with napari

Acquired images were split into single tiffs resulting in one tiff file per side, tile and channel using fiji (version 2.9.0 with java version 1.8.0). Images were loaded in a dataset with BigStitcher (version 0.8.3) using the Manual Loader and the naming convention “experiment_xx_side{a}-_tile{x}_ch{c}.tif.” for multiple tiles, angles and channels. Voxel size was loaded from file. Each of the tiff files was assigned a setup id which was later used for comparing different setups. The dataset was resaved as a HDF5 file for interactive viewing with BigDataViewer.

Within the datasets, first tiles were refined with ICP (chromatic aberration) and then stitched using the stitching mode. First tiles were moved to a regular grid specifying their order and overlap. Then Pairwise Shifts were calculated with Phase correlation over averaged channels and with 2×2×2 downsampling for 1024×1024px images and 4×4×2 for 2048×2048px images. Pairwise shifts were explored with the Interactive Link Explorer, only links with R value over 0.7 were selected and Global Optimization with Simple One-Round was run for stitching. After that interest points were detected in all channels with Difference-of-Gaussian, grouped tiles and 3-dimensial quadratic fit utilizing the TetraSpeck™ beads. Parameters were set interactively. The threshold was set until most beads were detected. For 0.2 μm beads a sigma of 1.8015 was used. Bead labels were detected separately for each channel to optimize detection parameters for each channel, but labeling was kept the same to enable grouped registration throughout all channels.

All sides were registered using the fast descriptor-based (rotation invariant) algorithm and the bead label represented in all views. All views were compared to each other with grouped tiles, fixed first view and no map back. The transformation model selected was affine with regularize model. Redundancy for descriptor matching was set to 0, Significance for a descriptor match to 10, allowed error for RANSAC (px): 5 and Number of RANSAC iterations: Normal. A rigid model was used to regularize with Lamba: 0.1. Interest points were not grouped, and views were computed independently. After registration, a Bounding Box was defined to cover the embryo. After that, images were fused within a pre-defined Bounding Box using Linear Interpolation with a downsampling of 1, pixel type: 16-bit unsigned integer. Fused images can also be exported as other formats to be compatible with interactive viewers like BigDataViewer. Detailed BigStitcher instructions can be found here.17 In general, sample based features like nuclei can be used for alignment as well and offer a way of improving the bead-based alignment.21

For error mapping a python script for comparing a set of setup ids was used. The script used the interest point coordinates of each setup together with respective transformation matrices stored in the dataset. After calculating the global coordinates of the interest points, distances between corresponding beads were calculated and plotted in 3d using the napari points layer. The script can be found under https://github.com/smegason/SMIM.

## Abstract

Endosomal trafficking of receptors and associated proteins plays a critical role in signal processing. Until recently, it was thought that trafficking was shut down during cell division. Thus, remarkably, the regulation of trafficking during division remains poorly characterized. Here we delineate the role of mitotic kinases in receptor trafficking during asymmetric division. Targeted perturbations reveal that Cyclin-dependent Kinase 1 (CDK1) and Aurora Kinase promote storage of Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptors (FGFRs) by suppressing endosomal degradation and recycling pathways. As cells progress through metaphase, loss of CDK1 activity permits differential degradation and targeted recycling of stored receptors, leading to asymmetric induction. Mitotic receptor storage, as delineated in this study, may facilitate rapid reestablishment of signaling competence in nascent daughter cells. However, mutations that limit or enhance the release of stored signaling components could alter daughter cell fate or behavior thereby promoting oncogenesis.

## Introduction

Dividing cells undergo dynamic shifts in membrane trafficking. During mitotic entry, internalization of plasma membrane promotes cell rounding [1]. As cells exit mitosis, targeted recycling promotes formation of the cytokinetic furrow [2,3]. Membrane and associated integral membrane proteins are trafficked through a well-delineated system of endosomal compartments [1,4]. In this endosomal trafficking network, Rab GTPases dictate compartment-specific functions (Fig 1A). Newly endocytosed vesicles fuse to form early endosomes distinguished by RAB4 and RAB5. These early endosomes can either recycle back to the plasma membrane through RAB4-dependent fast recycling or mature into late endosomes through a RAB7-dependent pathway. Recycling can also occur through a slow, RAB11-dependent pathway. Late endosomes eventually fuse with lysosomes leading to degradation of integral membrane proteins and other cargo [5]. Bulk internalization during entry appears to be mediated by suppression of recycling rather than an increase in endocytosis, but the specific endocytic pathways involved in entry trafficking have not been identified [1]. Recent studies have begun to reveal essential roles for mitotic membrane trafficking in tissue homeostasis and embryonic patterning. In the mammalian epidermis, symmetrically dividing cells internalize Ceslr1 (Cadherin EGF LAG seven-pass G-type receptor 1) and other membrane proteins involved in planar cell polarization. Unbiased redistribution of these internalized proteins during mitotic exit appears to be critical for reintegration of dividing cells into the epithelium [9]. In the developing wing of Drosophila embryos, unbiased redistribution of transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) receptors internalized during mitotic entry ensures proper patterning [10]. In a range of asymmetrically dividing embryonic and stem cell lineages, integral membrane proteins involved in Notch signaling are internalized during mitosis [11–13]. Biased redistribution of these signaling components during mitotic exit underlies asymmetric fate specification. Despite the importance of mitotic trafficking in embryonic patterning and tissue integrity, insights into the regulatory hierarchy choreographing the uptake and redistribution of signaling components remain extremely limited. Mitosis is choreographed by 3 major classes of mitotic kinases, CDK1, Aurora Kinases (AurKs), and Polo-like Kinases (PLKs) [14]. During mitotic entry, these kinases regulate a diverse set of cellular processes required for spindle assembly, centrosome dynamics, chromatid separation, and cytokinesis. As cells progress through metaphase, Cyclin B is degraded, and the resulting loss of CDK1 activity is critical for promoting exit-specific cellular processes. Remarkably, due in part to the long-standing assumption that trafficking was shut down during mitosis [2,3,15–17], very few studies have addressed the regulatory roles of these kinases in mitotic trafficking. Exceptions include research on the mammalian epidermis demonstrating that PLK1-dependent phosphorylation of the planar cell polarity protein Celsr1 mediates mitotic internalization [18]. In yeast, PLK1 has also been reported to phosphorylate ESCRT (endosomal sorting complexes required for transport) proteins required for septation [19]. Poor characterization of the regulatory links between mitotic kinases and division-specific trafficking patterns represents a fundamental gap in our understanding of the interplay between cell division and signaling. We have begun to address this gap by studying cranial-cardiac progenitor specification in the invertebrate chordate, Ciona intestinalis (Type A, also referred to as Ciona robusta). In Ciona embryos, the heart is derived from a set of 4 precardiac founder cells. Each founder cell divides asymmetrically to produce 1 cranial-cardiac progenitor (or trunk ventral cell, TVC) and 1 tail muscle progenitor (Fig 1A; [20,21]). Fibroblast Growth Factor (FGF) receptors are unequally distributed during founder cell division [20]. Immediately following division, differential inheritance of FGF receptors generates asymmetric FGF-dependent induction of cranial-cardiac progenitor cell fate [21–23]. Localized cell–matrix adhesion biases mitotic FGFR redistribution through localized retention and/or recycling of Caveolin-rich membrane domains and associated FGF receptors [20]. By characterizing the regulation of mitotic FGFR redistribution in Ciona founder cells, we aim to reveal more general mechanisms for mitotic trafficking and explore how these mechanisms are biased during asymmetric divisions.

## CDK1 suppresses FGFR degradation during mitotic entry

We next sought to investigate the role of the primary mitotic entry kinase, CDK1, in FGFR trafficking (Fig 3). By treating late gastrulae (Hotta Stage 14) with a fast-acting CDK1 inhibitor (roscovitine/seliciclib), we were able to block CDK1 activity in mitotic founder cells. Through DRAQ5 staining, we were able to identify treated founder cells displaying chromatin condensation, indicating that they had been arrested in prophase. We began investigating the impact of this treatment on FGFR trafficking using transgenic Mesp>FGFR::Venus, Mesp>CLIP:: Rab7 embryos. Intriguingly, arrested founder cells displayed a dramatic decrease in FGFR:: VENUS staining (Fig 3A, 3B’ and 3E). To investigate whether the observed reduction in FGFR::VENUS was a nonspecific result of mitotic arrest, we treated founder cells with AurK inhibitors (Aurora A/B inhibitor: VX-680 or Pan-Aurora Kinase inhibitor: AMG-900). Because these drugs act relatively slowly, we treated embryos just prior to founder cell division (Hotta Stage 13). Treatment with either inhibitor at this stage resulted in prophase arrest, but there was no discernable reduction in FGFR::VENUS staining (VX680, Fig 3C–3C’). We used the same assay to examine the impact of roscovitine treatment on another integral membrane protein, E-CADHERIN::GFP (Mesp>E-Cadherin::GFP; Fig 3F–3H). In contrast with the FGFR::VENUS results, roscovitine treatment had no discernable impact on E-CADHERIN:: GFP staining. ## Discussion

Based on our data, we propose a new model for mitotic regulation of FGFR trafficking (Fig 6). According to our model, CDK1 and AurK synergize to promote FGFR storage during mitotic entry. We propose that mitotic receptor storage generates 2 functionally discrete pools. One pool consists of FGF receptor-enriched vesicles shunted into either fast or slow recycling pathways. CDK1 and AurK maintain this pool by suppressing recycling pathways. The second pool consists of FGFR-enriched vesicles that have been shunted into the maturation pathway. CDK1 maintains this pool by suppressing degradation. As cells exit division, the associated inactivation of CDK1 releases both pools of accumulated receptors. Reinitiation of fast recycling restores receptor enrichment on the plasma membrane. Reinitiation of degradation may bias this process, leading to nonuniform receptor redistribution. In Ciona founder cells, it appears that matrix adhesion polarizes FGFR trafficking during mitosis, leading to elevated receptor accumulation on the nascent heart progenitor membrane and differential induction (Fig 1A, [20]). Our current model posits that integrin-dependent enrichment of caveolin within adhesive membranes dictates polarized FGFR trafficking [20]. Current studies are focused on determining the specific contributions of integrin and caveolin to this process. We are also investigating whether adhesion suppresses FGFR degradation or promotes FGFR recycling, thereby biasing the redistribution of “stored” FGFR during mitotic exit (Fig 6). Previous studies suggest that PLK1-mediated activation of slow recycling may also contribute to receptor recycling and/or receptor redistribution [18,19]. We are currently exploring whether this conserved role for PLK1 overcomes AurK-dependent suppression of slow recycling (Fig 2D and 2F’) to promote delivery of FGF receptors from the RAB11 recycling compartment to the plasma membrane as illustrated in our model (Fig 6). Our data also suggest that the previously characterized CDK1-dependent phosphorylation of RAB4 [28] directly suppresses RAB4-mediated recycling during mitotic entry (Fig 4E–4K). This regulatory relationship appears to be broadly conserved as indicted by sequence conservation of the CDK1 phosphorylation site across a wide range of vertebrate Rab4a genes, along with orthologous genes from a variety of tunicates (including Ciona, Fig 4E) amphioxus, echinoderms, mollusks, cnidarians, and even potentially in slime molds. Interestingly, this phosphorylation site does not appear to be conserved in vertebrate Rab4b genes, although they do contain a potential alternate CDK1 phosphorylation site. We also hypothesize that CDK1-dependent suppression of fast recycling may be a general feature of mitotic entry deployed in a wide variety of cell types to reduce membrane surface area during mitotic rounding which leads, incidentally, to storage and sequestration of associated membrane proteins. We are also currently exploring whether other key regulatory nodes in our model involve direct interactions between the mitotic kinases and Rab GTPases or if they involve a more complex regulatory circuit. For instance, AurK may suppress slow recycling through direct phosphorylation of—Rab11, Rab 11 effectors such as FIPs, Myosin VB, the kinesin Kif13A, or the exocyst subunit EXOC6 [4,32]. Alternatively, AurK may directly disrupt downstream factors associated with delivery of slow recycling endosomes to the plasma membrane including Arf6 and its effectors [33]. Additionally, our data indicate that CDK1 specifically suppresses degradation for a subset of membrane proteins, including FGFR, rather than uniformly influencing the degradation pathway (Fig 3F–3H). We are currently investigating the range of receptors subjected to the mitotic trafficking pathways we have identified and the molecular basis for this selectivity. Mitotic receptor storage, as delineated in this study, poses a number of potential benefits and risks. Suppression of lysosomal degradation may facilitate retention of signaling components allowing daughter cells to rapidly reacquire signaling competence. In asymmetrically dividing cells, stored receptors can be rapidly redistributed in response to polarized intrinsic or extrinsic cues generating robust asymmetry in nascent daughter cells. Furthermore, mitotic internalization may serve to sequester receptors during the dynamic process of cell division and prevent spurious signaling. Cell rounding during mitotic entry entails extensive remodeling of the cell membrane and actin cortex along with disassembly of cell–cell and cell–matrix adhesions [36]. Thus, signal modulation provided by membrane microdomains [37,38] or by extensive cross-talk between adhesion and signaling complexes [39] are compromised in dividing cells. Moreover, alterations in cell composition and morphology associated with tissue growth and repair can dramatically alter the signaling environment of dividing cells exacerbating the potential for signal misinterpretation. Thus, sequestration of growth factor receptors during division may play a key role in the suppression of unintended signaling and associated oncogenic behaviors. Conversely, mutations that lead to precocious release of stored receptors could reverse this sequestration and promote oncogenesis.
